T1: Consumers will adopt Jotun’s marine and protective coatings for home improvement projects if they perceive the technology as a premium, durable solution that protects assets (e.g., boats, outdoor gear) and reduces maintenance costs. Who benefits: Homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who own boats, outdoor equipment, or want long‑lasting protective finishes.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view marine coatings as a high‑performance, long‑lasting alternative to standard paints, they will choose Jotun for projects requiring durability and protection.. How value is captured: Jotun would capture value by selling premium‑priced coatings directly to consumers through retail channels or online, earning higher margins than bulk B2B sales.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for marine‑grade durability.; Jotun can market the technology effectively to DIY audiences.; Retail distribution is feasible and cost‑effective.. Predictions: In a test offering Jotun marine coatings for home boats/outdoor gear at a 20% price premium, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than a standard paint alternative.; Surveyed consumers will cite durability and protection as primary reasons for choosing Jotun..

T2: Consumers will adopt Jotun’s marine and protective coatings for home improvement projects if they perceive the technology as a status‑enhancing, premium product that signals lifestyle and design sophistication. Who benefits: Affluent homeowners and design‑conscious consumers who use home improvement as a way to express personal style and social status.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view marine coatings as a high‑end, design‑focused product, they will choose Jotun to elevate the aesthetic and social value of their projects.. How value is captured: Jotun would capture value by pricing premium coatings at a higher margin and selling through design‑focused retail channels or online marketplaces that emphasize lifestyle branding.. Assumptions: Affluent consumers are willing to pay a premium for design‑enhancing finishes.; Jotun can position its coatings as a lifestyle product through marketing and design partnerships.; Retail distribution in design‑focused stores is feasible.. Predictions: In a test offering Jotun marine coatings for home projects at a 15% price premium, purchase intent among affluent consumers will be at least 10% higher than a standard paint alternative.; Surveyed consumers will cite design appeal and status as primary reasons for choosing Jotun..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Durability vs Status Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants view a product description of Jotun marine coating for home boats/outdoor gear, presented with either durability-focused messaging (e.g., "Protect your assets with marine-grade durability") or status/design-focused messaging (e.g., "Elevate your home with premium, design-conscious marine coating"). They are then asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay (WTP) and their likelihood to purchase. The test will. Sample: 300 Norwegian and Swedish consumers aged 25-55 who own boats, outdoor gear, or have home improvement projects. Recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic coverage.. Measure: Primary outcome: average WTP difference between durability and status messaging groups. Secondary outcomes: purchase intent (binary) and stated importance of durability/status.. Predictions: T1: Durability messaging will generate a higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than status messaging.; T2: Status messaging will generate a higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than durability messaging.. Decision rule: If the average WTP difference between groups is at least 15% (e.g., durability group WTP €120, status group WTP €100), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting durability. If the difference is less than 10%. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure whether durability messaging drives higher willingness-to-pay and purchase intent than status messaging. If the test shows a ≥15% WTP difference in favor of durability, proceed to develop a durability-focused proposition; otherwise, maintain the B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure whether durability messaging drives higher willingness-to-pay and purchase intent than status messaging. If the test shows a ≥15% WTP difference in favor of durability, proceed to develop a durability-focused proposition; otherwise, maintain the B2B focus. Target customer: Homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who own boats, outdoor gear, or want long‑lasting protective finishes.. Value proposition: A Jotun marine coating proposition that emphasizes durability, protection, and premium performance for home improvement projects, sold through retail channels or online with a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeline and €18,000 budget, measuring willingness-to-pay and purchase intent under durability and status messaging.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer survey data; the test is needed to resolve which messaging drives higher WTP and purchase intent.. Would change if: If the test shows a ≥15% WTP advantage for durability messaging, indicating consumer preference for durability over status.; If additional evidence shows that affluent consumers are willing to pay a premium for design appeal, shifting support toward T2.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: The device, when it is a body composition analyzer which is not intended to diagnose or treat any medical condition, is exempt from the premarket notification procedures in subpart E of part 807 of this chapter

Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers, Tanita introduced the world’s first integrated body composition analyzer/scale to the professional markets in 1992.
Tanita is a world leader in precision electronic scales. With almost 50% of its domestic market share, the name Tanita is a household name in Japan.
In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.
In 104 men and 101 women (16-78 years and BMI 16-41 kg/m2) the mean bias in body-fat mass measured using the Tanita body-fat analyser was 0.8 (2SD 7.9) kg relative to a four-compartment model.

T1: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for home use because they value precise, non-invasive health monitoring and are willing to pay a premium for data that predicts disease risk. Who benefits: Consumers seeking personal health insights; Tanita benefits by capturing premium pricing and recurring data services.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of body composition as a health predictor (e.g., heart disease, diabetes) creates demand for accurate, easy-to-use home tools.. How value is captured: Tanita sells the device at a premium price and offers subscription services for data interpretation and personalized recommendations.. Assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a reliable method for body-fat measurement.; There is sufficient disposable income among target consumers to purchase a home analyser.; Marketing can effectively communicate health benefits and differentiate Tanita from competitors.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase at a price point above standard scales.; Pilot sales of a consumer version will generate recurring revenue from data subscriptions within 12 months.; Competitor devices will show lower accuracy or lack health-risk reporting, making Tanita's proposition more attractive..

T2: Health insurance providers will subsidize or require a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for policyholders because it reduces claims costs by enabling early detection of obesity-related conditions, creating demand for volume purchases. Who benefits: Insurance providers gain cost savings and compliance; Tanita benefits by selling through insurers and potentially receiving volume discounts.. Why behaviour changes: Insurance companies increasingly use preventive care to lower long-term costs; a device that predicts obesity and associated diseases becomes a cost-saving tool for insurers.. How value is captured: Tanita sells devices at volume to insurers at a lower price point, and may receive recurring revenue from data services or subscription fees for interpretation.. Assumptions: Insurance providers are willing to invest in preventive devices that demonstrably reduce claims.; Regulatory environment in 1993 allows insurers to subsidize health-promoting products.; Tanita can meet any data privacy or security requirements insurers impose.. Predictions: Insurance providers will place orders for devices in quantities sufficient to secure volume discounts.; Pilot programs with insurers will show a measurable reduction in obesity-related claims within 12 months.; Competitor devices without insurer backing will struggle to gain market share..

Why behaviour changes: These users already carry safety gear and are aware of the risk of isolation; a distress beacon that uses the established 406 MHz frequency and is certified for emergency use will be perceived as a necessary addition to their kit.. T2: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are willing to pay a premium for a brand associated with agricultural excellence and reliability, and they trust Deere's engineering heritage. Why behaviour changes: Deere's strong reputation in the agricultural sector creates a halo effect that transfers to consumer products, making homeowners more willing to purchase a lawn tractor even at a higher price point.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by positioning the lawn tractor as a premium, brand-trusted product, commanding higher prices and selling through the existing dealer network that already carries agricultural equipment.. Assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 associate Deere with high-quality agricultural machinery.; Deere's brand reputation is sufficient to overcome price sensitivity for a consumer product.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a brand they trust in other contexts.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing its agricultural heritage and reliability, dealer sales will increase relative to a baseline period without the proposition.; Surveyed homeowners will rank "brand trust" as a top purchase criterion for a lawn and garden tractor..

Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a convenience-focused proposition (multiple-task capability, affordability) or a brand-trust proposition (agricultural heritage, reliability). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale and rank willingness to pay.. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 30–65 who own or rent a property with a yard, recruited via an online panel. Randomly assigned to either convenience or brand trust condition (250 per group).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (WTP) amount in euros.. Predictions: T1: Participants exposed to the convenience proposition will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than those exposed to the brand trust proposition.; T2: Participants exposed to the brand trust proposition will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than those exposed to the convenience proposition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the convenience group exceeds the brand trust group by at least 1.5 points on the 10‑point scale AND the average WTP for the convenience group exceeds the brand trust group by at least 10 euros, then T1 is supported. If the opposite. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Because of this, many John Deere dealers were selling some of these lines or other brands of lawn and garden tractors because Deere didn’t offer any.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Price vs. Prestige Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are homeowners with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) who have never owned a lawn and garden tractor. They are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing price (e.g., $500, "inexpensive, practical for a variety of chores, economical to maintain"); Group B sees a product description emphasizing prestige (e.g., $700, "modern household amenity, signals ownership of a progressive household, convenient for small gardens"). Both groups view the same product image and are asked: "Would you purchase this tractor?" (Yes/No) and "What is the maximum price you would pay?" (open number).. Sample: 200 participants (100 per group) recruited via an online panel of homeowners in the United States. Inclusion criteria: age 30-65, own a home with a small garden (<1/4 acre), have never owned a lawn and garden tractor.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum price willing to pay (numeric). Secondary measure: self-reported importance of price vs. prestige (1-5 scale).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher maximum price than Group B, because price-sensitive homeowners will respond to the inexpensive positioning.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher maximum price than Group A, because prestige-driven homeowners will respond to the status positioning.. T1: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for home use because they value precise, non-invasive health monitoring and are willing to pay a premium for data that predicts disease risk. Who benefits: Consumers seeking personal health insights; Tanita benefits by capturing premium pricing and recurring data services.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of body composition as a health predictor (e.g., heart disease, diabetes) creates demand for accurate, easy-to-use home tools.. How value is captured: Tanita sells the device at a premium price and offers subscription services for data interpretation and personalized recommendations.. Assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a reliable method for body-fat measurement.; There is sufficient disposable income among target consumers to purchase a home analyser.; Marketing can effectively communicate health benefits and differentiate Tanita from competitors.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase at a price point above standard scales.; Pilot sales of a home version will generate recurring revenue from data subscriptions within 12 months.; Competitor devices will show lower accuracy or lack health-risk reporting, making Tanita's proposition more attractive..

T2: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for home use because they value convenience and privacy, and are willing to pay for a non-invasive, quick measurement that can be done at home without professional supervision. Who benefits: Consumers seeking easy, private health checks; Tanita benefits by capturing sales volume and data subscriptions.. Why behaviour changes: Growing preference for self-monitoring and desire to avoid public exposure of health data create demand for home devices that offer immediate results.. How value is captured: Tanita sells the device at a modest price point and offers optional data storage and interpretation services, generating recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers trust the accuracy of bioelectrical impedance for body-fat measurement.; Privacy concerns outweigh cost differences compared to clinic visits.; Marketing can emphasize home convenience and speed of results.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase at a price point below clinic-level devices.; Pilot sales will be higher in regions with limited clinic access or long wait times.; Competitor devices marketed as "clinic-grade" will be perceived as unnecessary for home use, making Tanita's proposition more attractive..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection proposition if they perceive it as a fashion or lifestyle accessory that signals status and personal expression. Who benefits: Fashion-conscious consumers seeking visible protection; Hellberg would capture value through premium pricing and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a visible, stylish product, they will be willing to purchase multiple units and share on social media, creating a personal-expression market.. How value is captured: Hellberg can design limited-edition, color-coded, or customizable hearing protectors and sell them at a higher price point through direct-to-consumer channels, leveraging its existing brand.. Assumptions: Consumers in target segments (e.g., young professionals, outdoor enthusiasts) prioritize personal style over pure functionality.; Hellberg can maintain its brand image while offering differentiated aesthetic options.; There is sufficient willingness to pay a premium for visible hearing protection.. Predictions: In a test offering a fashion-focused hearing protector at 1.5x the price of standard models, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than for a standard model.; Social media engagement (shares, comments) for the fashion version will be at least 20% higher than for the standard version..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection proposition if they need it for a specific, high-risk activity (e.g., industrial work, hunting, music) and perceive the product as a safety-critical tool that meets that need. Who benefits: Safety-conscious professionals and enthusiasts who require reliable protection for specific tasks; Hellberg would capture value through premium pricing and specialized marketing.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a necessary safety item for a specific activity, they will prioritize purchasing a product that is clearly designed for that use case, even if it is more expensive.. How value is captured: Hellberg can develop specialized hearing protectors for industrial, hunting, or music use, positioning them as essential safety gear, and sell them at premium prices through targeted B2B and niche channels.. Assumptions: There is a measurable demand for specialized hearing protection in target segments.; Consumers in these segments are willing to pay a premium for a product that explicitly addresses their safety need.; Hellberg can design products that meet the specific requirements of each use case.. Predictions: In a test offering a specialized hearing protector for industrial workers at 1.2x the price of standard models, purchase intent among industrial buyers will be at least 10% higher than for a standard model.; Safety ratings (e.g., EN 352) will be cited in at least 70% of reviews for the specialized version..

Test "Fashion vs Safety Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to either a fashion-focused hearing protector or a safety-focused hearing protector, followed by willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent questions.. Sample: 500 Swedish adults aged 18-45, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and interest in outdoor activities.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?") 2) Willingness-to-pay (EUR amount entered) 3) Self-reported importance of fashion vs safety (1-5 scale) 4) Social media sharing intent (binary: "Would you share a photo of this product on social media?"). Predictions: T1: Fashion version will show at least 15% higher purchase intent and willingness-to-pay than the safety version.; T2: Safety version will show at least 10% higher purchase intent and willingness-to-pay than the fashion version.. Decision rule: If the fashion version’s purchase intent exceeds the safety version’s by ≥ 15 percentage points AND the safety version’s purchase intent exceeds the fashion version’s by ≥ 10 percentage points, we conclude both theories are supported. If only T1 is supported, we recommend a fashion-focused consumer proposition; if only T2 is supported, we recommend a safety-focused proposition; if neither is supported, we recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Dealer Survey Test" between T1; T2. Method: Survey existing John Deere dealers in the United States about their willingness to stock a new lawn and garden tractor. Randomly assign dealers to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of a standard, low‑priced lawn and garden tractor (price comparable to competitors) and a brief description of Deere’s existing dealer network. Group B receives the same description plus a statement emphasizing Deere’s agricultural brand trust and premium positioning (price 20% above competitors). Both groups are asked: "Would you stock this product in your. Sample: 200 John Deere dealers across the United States, selected from the company’s dealer directory, stratified by region.. Measure: Percentage of dealers in each group who indicate they would stock the product.. Predictions: T1: Group A’s willingness to stock will be at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B’s, because the low‑priced proposition aligns with existing dealer network and consumer demand.; T2: Group B’s willingness to stock will be at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A’s, because the premium brand positioning justifies a higher price and aligns with dealer trust in Deere.. Decision rule: If Group A’s willingness to stock is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B’s, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small‑garden households (supports T1). If Group B’s willingness to stock is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A’s, proceed with a premium. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed Dealer Survey Test (X1) to measure willingness to stock a low‑priced lawn and garden tractor versus a premium‑branded version. If the test shows a ≥15‑percentage‑point advantage for the low‑priced proposition, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small‑garden households; otherwise, reconsider expansion or focus on existing dealer network. The test is affordable (€15,000)  Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, brand trust, or dealer willingness to stock a lawn and garden tractor. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they perceive them as a practical, inexpensive tool for multiple tasks, and they can purchase through existing dealer networks without requiring new channels.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Conduct the proposed Dealer Survey Test (X1) to measure willingness to stock a low‑priced lawn and garden tractor versus a premium‑branded version. If the test shows a ≥15‑percentage‑point advantage for the low‑priced proposition, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small‑garden households; otherwise, reconsider expansion or focus on existing dealer network. The test is affordable (€15,000)  Target customer: Small‑garden households (households with small gardens that need a versatile, inexpensive tool for multiple chores).. Value proposition: A differentiated lawn and garden tractor leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network, offering a practical, low‑cost solution for small‑garden tasks, while maintaining the brand’s reputation for agricultural quality.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Dealer Survey Test (200 dealers, 10 weeks, €15,000).. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence from 1962 about consumer demand, dealer willingness, or brand trust. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows a ≥15‑percentage‑point advantage for the premium‑branded version, shift focus to a premium consumer proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or a disadvantage for either proposition, recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the existing dealer model.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.; Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.; 2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.; 4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers)..

T1: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and easy to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking affordable, versatile garden tools; Deere benefits by selling tractors directly or through dealers, capturing higher margins than bulk farm equipment.. Why behaviour changes: Rapidly rising sales of garden tractors (76% growth 1960-1979) indicates homeowners shift from manual tools to powered equipment; the low cost and multi-use capability make the shift attractive.. How value is captured: Deere can price tractors modestly and sell accessories, earning revenue from a new consumer segment while leveraging existing tractor engineering.. Assumptions: Small-garden homeowners have sufficient disposable income to purchase a tractor.; They value time-saving and multi-use functionality.; Deere can reach this segment through existing dealer network or new direct channels.. Predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay a price point comparable to early 1960s consumer goods for a garden tractor.; Pilot sales of a basic garden tractor will exceed dealer expectations within 12 weeks.; Accessory sales (e.g., mower blades, snow blowers) will be higher than for farm tractors..

T2: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they represent a new, convenient way to perform yard work, and the low cost of entry makes it attractive for occasional use, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking a quick, affordable solution for yard tasks; Deere benefits by selling a small, low-margin tractor and accessories, expanding its consumer reach.. Why behaviour changes: The rise of suburban home ownership and the desire for neat yards create a market for convenient yard tools; the low price point makes the tractor accessible for occasional use, shifting from manual to powered tools.. How value is captured: Deere can sell a basic tractor at a modest price and bundle accessories, generating revenue from a new segment while leveraging existing tractor technology.. Assumptions: Suburban homeowners have limited yard space and time for extensive gardening.; They value convenience and low cost for occasional yard work.; Deere can reach this segment through existing dealer network or new direct channels.. Predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to purchase a tractor priced at a level comparable to 1960s consumer goods for occasional yard work.; Pilot sales of a basic garden tractor will exceed dealer expectations within 12 weeks when marketed as a convenient, low-cost solution.; Accessory sales (e.g., mower blades, snow blowers) will be higher than for farm tractors because users need consumables for occasional use..

Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Garden Tractor Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two versions of a product description: Version A emphasizes affordability, practicality for small gardens, and low maintenance; Version B emphasizes convenience, occasional yard work, and low cost entry. Both versions include a price point of $1,200 (1962 dollars). Participants are asked: "Would you purchase this garden tractor?" (Yes/No) and "How likely are you to purchase it?" (1‑10).. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25–65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region.. Measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and likelihood score (1‑10). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in 1962 dollars.. Predictions: T1: Version A will achieve higher purchase intent and likelihood than Version B because homeowners with small gardens value affordability and practicality.; T2: Version B will achieve higher purchase intent and likelihood than Version A because homeowners value convenience and low-cost entry for occasional yard work.. Decision rule: If Version A’s purchase intent exceeds Version B’s by at least 5 percentage points (e.g., 35% vs. 30%), proceed with the differentiated consumer proposition targeting small‑garden homeowners. If Version B exceeds Version A by at least 5 percentage points (e.g., 35% vs. 30%),. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate demand before committing resources. If the survey shows Version A (affordability/practicality) outperforms Version B (convenience/low cost) by at least 5 percentage points, proceed to develop a small‑garden‑focused consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain the existing dealer model. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection proposition if they perceive it as a fashion or lifestyle accessory, because they will own multiple pairs for different activities and are willing to pay a premium. Who benefits: Consumers seeking status and variety; Hellberg Safety through higher-margin sales and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: If hearing protection is marketed as a stylish, comfortable accessory rather than a medical necessity, consumers will view it as a personal choice and will purchase multiple units for different contexts (e.g., work, leisure, travel).. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by selling premium-priced, design-focused models directly to consumers, leveraging its existing e-commerce platform and brand reputation.. Assumptions: Consumers in target markets (e.g., urban professionals, outdoor enthusiasts) value aesthetics and convenience.; Hellberg can design and produce fashionable hearing protection without compromising safety.; The price premium for fashion-oriented models will be accepted by the target segment.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to buy multiple pairs for different scenarios.; Sales of a fashion-focused line will be higher than baseline hearing-protection sales in the same market.; Brand perception surveys will show higher association with style and status than with safety alone..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection proposition if they need it for a specific, high-risk activity (e.g., industrial work, shooting sports) and find Hellberg offers superior safety performance, because they prioritize protection over fashion. Who benefits: Safety-conscious consumers and Hellberg through premium pricing and brand positioning as the industry leader.. Why behaviour changes: If Hellberg can demonstrate superior safety features, noise reduction, or compliance with industry standards, consumers will choose its products even if they are not marketed as fashion items, because safety is the primary purchase driver.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by pricing based on safety performance, leveraging its existing B2B relationships and regulatory compliance reputation to justify higher prices.. Assumptions: There is a segment of consumers who research safety ratings and are willing to pay more for proven protection.; Hellberg’s current safety reputation is sufficient to attract this segment.; The product can be positioned as a safety-critical item without compromising fashion appeal.. Predictions: Surveyed safety-conscious consumers will indicate intent to purchase Hellberg for high-risk activities.; Sales of a safety-focused line will be higher in markets with high industrial or recreational activity.; Brand perception surveys will show higher association with safety and reliability than with style..

T1: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon because it provides a reliable, long-range emergency communication solution that is easier to use than existing methods (e.g., satellite phones, radio). Who benefits: Individual hikers, campers, and outdoor adventurers who need a lightweight, automatic distress signal device.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently rely on unreliable or cumbersome methods; a distress beacon that works with existing satellite networks and can be deployed without additional training would reduce risk and increase confidence in remote activities.. How value is captured: ACR can sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and build brand awareness among outdoor communities.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. were stable or growing in 2002.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety features that reduce risk.; Distribution channels (e.g., outdoor retailers) exist for direct-to-consumer sales.. Predictions: A survey of outdoor recreation groups would show >60% would consider purchasing a 406 MHz distress beacon.; Sales of the device would be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation density (e.g., national parks, mountain ranges)..

T2: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a standardized, reliable signal that can be detected across vast geographic areas, reducing response time and cost. Who benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, coast guards, and emergency management organizations that need to locate and assist remote individuals quickly.. Why behaviour changes: Current methods often rely on multiple frequencies and inconsistent signal strengths; a standardized 406 MHz beacon would simplify detection and coordination, leading to faster response and potentially saving lives.. case.question: It is 1993. Should Tanita develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for clinics and health clubs? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: The device, when it is a body composition analyzer which is not intended to diagnose or treat any medical condition, is exempt from the premarket notification procedures in subpart E of part 807 of this chapter

Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers, Tanita introduced the world’s first integrated body composition analyzer/scale to the professional markets in 1992.
Tanita is a world leader in precision electronic scales. With almost 50% of its domestic market share, the name Tanita is a household name in Japan.
In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.

A body fat measuring apparatus for measuring body fat in a patient's body comprises apparatus for simultaneously measuring an impedance between the patient's feet, and for measuring the patient's height and the patient's weight
In 104 men and 101 women (16-78 years and BMI 16-41 kg/m2) the mean bias in body-fat mass measured using the Tanita body-fat analyser was 0.8 (2SD 7.9) kg relative to a four-compartment model.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.; Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users for personal health monitoring.; 2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product line without a new consumer proposition (status quo).; 3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group, such as partnering with retailers or targeting corporate wellness programs.; 4) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B customers..

T1: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for home use because they value precise, non-invasive measurement of body composition for personal health monitoring. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking to track health and body composition.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of the health risks associated with excess body fat (as indicated by medical evidence and media coverage) creates a demand for accurate, easy-to-use home measurement tools.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value by selling the analyser directly to consumers at a premium price, leveraging its existing brand trust and clinical validation.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Tanita’s clinical reputation and are willing to pay for precise body-fat data.; Home use is feasible and convenient for target consumers (e.g., those with access to a bathroom scale).; Regulatory clearance for home use is achievable based on existing medical device status.. Predictions: If offered a home version, a measurable share of existing clinic/health club customers would purchase it.; Surveyed consumers would indicate willingness to pay a price premium for accurate body-fat data.; Sales of the home version would correlate with broader consumer awareness campaigns about body composition health..

T2: Consumers will adopt a stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for home use because they seek convenience and privacy, avoiding the stigma or embarrassment associated with traditional clinical measurements. Who benefits: Individual consumers who prefer non-clinical, private measurement of body composition.. Why behaviour changes: Stigma around body measurements in clinical settings (e.g., doctors’ offices) creates a preference for home-based, discreet solutions.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value by positioning the analyser as a private, convenient tool, potentially at a lower price point than clinical models, and through retail distribution.. Assumptions: Privacy concerns outweigh cost for target consumers.; Home use is convenient and accessible for target demographic.; Regulatory clearance for home use is achievable without major changes.. Predictions: If offered a home version, a segment of existing clinic/health club customers would purchase it for personal use.; Surveyed consumers would rank privacy higher than accuracy when choosing a body-fat device.; Sales would be driven by marketing that emphasizes home convenience and discretion..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Privacy vs. Accuracy Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two product descriptions: (1) stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser marketed for home use with emphasis on precision and clinical accuracy; (2) same analyser marketed for home use with emphasis on privacy and convenience (e.g., discreet, private measurement). Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and choose which version they would buy. The test also collects demographic data.. Sample: 300 adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region. Inclusion: have used a scale to monitor body composition at least once in the past year.. Measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants choosing the precision-focused version versus the privacy-focused version. Secondary outcomes: average WTP for each version, and self-reported importance of privacy vs. accuracy.. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of participants will choose the precision-focused version, indicating demand driven by health monitoring.; T2: At least 60% will choose the privacy-focused version, indicating demand driven by convenience and stigma avoidance.. Decision rule: If the proportion choosing the precision version ≥ 60% → proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing accuracy and clinical validation. If the proportion choosing the privacy version ≥ 60% → proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing privacy and convenience. If neither reaches 60% →. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure demand for a precision-focused version versus a privacy-focused version before committing resources. The test will clarify whether health-conscious demand (T1) or privacy/convenience demand (T2) drives consumer adoption, allowing a data-driven decision on product development. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure demand for a precision-focused version versus a privacy-focused version before committing resources. The test will clarify whether health-conscious demand (T1) or privacy/convenience demand (T2) drives consumer adoption, allowing a data-driven decision on product development. Target customer: Health-conscious consumers who value precise body-composition data for personal health monitoring, and potentially a secondary segment seeking convenience and privacy.. Value proposition: A stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser marketed as a home health monitor, emphasizing clinical accuracy and professional validation, sold at a premium price through existing distribution channels.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget to collect willingness-to-pay data and purchase intent for precision‑focused versus privacy‑focused versions.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a home version. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows ≥ 60% of participants choose the precision version, indicating strong health‑monitoring demand, we would proceed with a precision‑focused consumer proposition.; If the test shows ≥ 60% choose the privacy version, indicating strong convenience/privacy demand, we would explore a privacy‑focused proposition or a different route to market.; If neither threshold is met, we would recommend no expansion and maintain the existing B2B focus.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
